title: Section 1.6: Classifying Linear Equations (Part 2)
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 12 • Section 1.6 (Workbook p. 19)
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### The Three Types of Linear Equations (Workbook p. 19)
- **1. Conditional:** The equation has a **finite number of unique real solutions** (e.g. $x = 5$, $x = 0$). True under certain conditions.
- **2. Contradiction:** Variables cancel out leaving a **FALSE statement** (e.g. $0 = 7$). **NO SOLUTION ($\emptyset$)**.
- **3. Identity:** Variables cancel out leaving a **TRUE statement** (e.g. $5 = 5$, $0 = 0$). **ALL REAL NUMBERS ($\mathbb{R}$)**.
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Conditional: } & 2x = 6 \implies x = 3 \quad (\text{One unique solution}) \\
\text{Contradiction: } & x + 1 = x + 4 \implies 1 = 4 \quad (\text{False! No solution}) \\
\text{Identity: } & 2(x + 1) = 2x + 2 \implies 2x + 2 = 2x + 2 \quad (\text{True for all } x!)
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall: **Sora's Warning:** Don't confuse $x = 0$ (conditional, exactly 1 solution) with $0 = 5$ (contradiction, no solution)!
script:
[Prof. Park] Welcome everyone to Lecture 12 of M090 Introductory Algebra! I am Professor Eunju Park, and joining me at the teaching desk is TA Sora. Today, we explore Section 1.6 Part 2 on workbook page 19: Classifying Linear EquationsâConditional Equations, Contradictions, and Identities. Hello everyone!

[TA Sora] Up until now, every equation we solved gave us exactly one neat answer: x = 5, w = -9/4, or x = 0. These are called CONDITIONAL equations because the equation is true only under the specific condition that the variable equals that single number.

[Prof. Park] Most real-world engineering and business equations are conditional: if you want a bridge to carry 50 tons, the cable tension must equal exactly one specific value. But what happens when you solve an equation and the variable mysteriously DISAPPEARS from both sides?

[TA Sora] What does it mean when all the x's vanish into thin air? That is the big question today! When all variables cancel out, you are left comparing two numbers.

[Prof. Park] That leaves you with two distinct special possibilities: Possibility 1: You are left with a FALSE mathematical statement, like 0 = 7 or 12 = 25. Can zero ever equal seven? Of course not! That is a CONTRADICTION!

[TA Sora] When an equation leads to a contradiction, there is NO number in the entire universe that can make it true. We declare: NO SOLUTION, written with the empty set symbol, a circle with a slash through it: â.

[Prof. Park] Possibility 2: You are left with a TRUE mathematical statement, like 5 = 5 or 0 = 0. Does zero equal zero? Always! That is an IDENTITY! An identity is true for every number you could ever imagine.

[TA Sora] We declare: ALL REAL NUMBERS, written with the blackboard bold R symbol: â! Today, we will master classifying equations into these three families: Conditional (one solution), Contradiction (no solution), and Identity (all real numbers). Let's begin on slide 2!

[Prof. Park] Let's provide three real-world analogies to make the three equation types unforgettable: 1. Conditional equation: Imagine programming your GPS to drive to the Museum of the Rockies in Bozeman. There is one specific destination coordinate. The condition is met at that single point: x = 5. 2.

[TA Sora] Contradiction: Imagine setting your GPS to drive directly from Bozeman to Honolulu, Hawaii by car! No matter what route you try, you cannot drive across the Pacific Ocean! It is physically impossible. Contradiction = No Solution (â). 3.

[Prof. Park] Identity: Imagine asking: 'What points on the Yellowstone River are wet?' Every single drop of water on the entire river is wet! It is true by definition everywhere and for all time! Identity = All Real Numbers (â)! Those analogies make the concepts click immediately!

[TA Sora] Remember: when you are taking an exam, never just write down 'Identity' without stating the solution set! The classification is 'Identity,' but the actual solution is 'All Real Numbers' or â! Similarly, the classification is 'Contradiction,' but the solution is 'No Solution' or â!

title: Example 2C & 2D: Special Case Equations
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 12 • Section 1.6 Example 2C & 2D (Workbook p. 18)
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Solve each equation and classify (Workbook p. 18)
$$\text{C. } 2(7 - x) + 11 = 12 - 2x$$
$$\text{D. } -4 - (3 - x) - 2 = 9(x - 1) - 8x$$
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{Part\ C:}\quad & 14 - 2x + 11 = 12 - 2x \\
& 25 - 2x = 12 - 2x \\
& 25 - 2x + 2x = 12 - 2x + 2x \\
& \mathbf{25 = 12} \quad \text{\textbf{FALSE statement!}} \\
& \implies \mathbf{\text{Contradiction (No Solution, } \emptyset\text{)}} \\[1em]
\mathbf{Part\ D:}\quad & -4 - 3 + x - 2 = 9x - 9 - 8x \\
& x - 9 = x - 9 \\
& -9 = -9 \quad \text{\textbf{TRUE statement!}} \\
& \implies \mathbf{\text{Identity (All Real Numbers, } \mathbb{R}\text{)}}
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall: **What Happened to the Variable?** When the variable completely cancels out, look at the remaining numbers: False statement $\implies$ Contradiction. True statement $\implies$ Identity!
script:
[Prof. Park] On slide 2, let's examine Section 1.6 Examples 2C and 2D from workbook page 18: Solve each equation and classify it as conditional, contradiction, or identity. Let's solve Example 2C: 2(7 - x) + 11 = 12 - 2x.

[TA Sora] Step 1: Distribute 2 on the left side: 2 Â· 7 - 2 Â· x = 14 - 2x. So our equation is: 14 - 2x + 11 = 12 - 2x. Step 2: Combine like terms on the left: 14 + 11 = 25.

[Prof. Park] So we get: 25 - 2x = 12 - 2x. Step 3: Move variable terms to one side by adding 2x to both sides: 25 - 2x + 2x = 12 - 2x + 2x. Look what happens: -2x + 2x = 0 on BOTH sides!

[TA Sora] The variables completely vanish, leaving us with: 25 = 12! 25 = 12 is an absolute falsehood! 25 never equals 12! Because this statement is FALSE and the variable cancelled out, this equation is a CONTRADICTION! Our answer is: NO SOLUTION (or â).

[Prof. Park] In physical terms, this represents two parallel lines that never intersect, or two opposing physical forces that can never balance. Now let's solve Example 2D: -4 - (3 - x) - 2 = 9(x - 1) - 8x.

[TA Sora] Step 1: Distribute the negative sign on the left, and distribute 9 on the right: Left: -4 - 3 + x - 2. Right: 9x - 9 - 8x.

[Prof. Park] Step 2: Combine like terms on each side independently: Left side: -4 - 3 - 2 = -9, so we have: x - 9. Right side: 9x - 8x = x, so we have: x - 9.

[TA Sora] Notice that both sides are IDENTICAL: x - 9 = x - 9! If you subtract x from both sides: -9 = -9 (or add 9 to get 0 = 0). This is ALWAYS TRUE! Therefore, this equation is an IDENTITY!

[Prof. Park] Our answer is: ALL REAL NUMBERS (or â)! Let's also look at the geometric visualization of these special cases: In Unit 2, we will graph linear equations as straight lines on the Cartesian coordinate plane.

[TA Sora] A conditional equation represents two lines that intersect at one single point (x, y). A contradiction represents two parallel lines with the same slope that run side-by-side forever and never cross! Because they never meet, they share no points: No Solution!

[Prof. Park] An identity represents two equations that describe the exact same physical line lying directly on top of itself! Every single point on the line is a shared solution: All Real Numbers! Seeing algebra through geometry turns abstract symbols into visual maps.

[TA Sora] When the variables cancel and you see 25 = 12, your mental image should instantly be two parallel railroad tracks running through the Gallatin Canyon that never touch!

title: In-Class Practice #1 & #2
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 12 • Section 1.6 Extra Practice #1 & #2 (Workbook p. 19)
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Solve and classify (Workbook p. 19)
$$\text{1. } 3x - 2 = -9x + 15$$
$$\text{2. } r - 3 - 7 + r = 10 + 2r$$
pitfall: **Sign Watch in #2:** $-10$ does NOT equal $+10$! They are opposites, not equals. Hence it is a contradiction!
script:
[Prof. Park] Slide 3 takes us to In-Class Practice Problems 1 and 2 from workbook page 19: Problem 1: 3x - 2 = -9x + 15. Problem 2: r - 3 - 7 + r = 10 + 2r. Let's work Problem 1: 3x - 2 = -9x + 15.

[TA Sora] Let's move all x terms to the left by adding 9x to both sides: 3x + 9x - 2 = 15, which gives: 12x - 2 = 15. Add 2 to both sides: 12x = 15 + 2 = 17. Divide both sides by 12: x = 17/12!

[Prof. Park] Did the variable disappear? No! We found a single unique value: x = 17/12. Therefore, Problem 1 is classified as a CONDITIONAL equation! Exactly right. Now let's solve Problem 2: r - 3 - 7 + r = 10 + 2r.

[TA Sora] First, combine like terms on the left side: r + r = 2r. -3 - 7 = -10. So the left side is: 2r - 10. The right side is: 10 + 2r (or 2r + 10). So our equation is: 2r - 10 = 2r + 10.

[Prof. Park] Subtract 2r from both sides: 2r - 2r - 10 = 2r - 2r + 10. The r's cancel out completely: -10 = +10! Does negative 10 equal positive 10? No! Owing 10 dollars is definitely not the same as having 10 dollars in your wallet!

[TA Sora] This is a FALSE statement. Therefore, Problem 2 is a CONTRADICTION! Classification: Contradiction. Solution: No Solution (â). In Practice Problem 2, look at how the problem was disguised: r - 3 - 7 + r = 10 + 2r.

[Prof. Park] Before combining like terms, the left side looked completely different from the right side! Only after combining r + r into 2r and -3 - 7 into -10 did the true nature of the equation emerge: 2r - 10 = 2r + 10.

[TA Sora] Notice that both sides had 2r, but the constants were different (-10 vs +10). Whenever both sides have the EXACT same variable coefficient but DIFFERENT constant terms, the variables will inevitably cancel, creating an automatic contradiction! That is an expert pattern recognition tip, Sora!

[Prof. Park] If variable coefficients match but constants differ, you know immediately it's a contradiction without doing five lines of arithmetic! And look at Problem 1: 3x - 2 = -9x + 15. The coefficients were +3 and -9. Since +3 does not equal -9, the variable CANNOT cancel out!

[TA Sora] It is guaranteed to be conditional. Checking variable coefficients before you calculate saves mental energy on exams!

title: In-Class Practice #3 & #4
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 12 • Section 1.6 Extra Practice #3 & #4 (Workbook p. 19)
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
pitfall: **Distribute fully in #3:** $3(w-9) = 3w - 27$. Then $-27 + 15 = -12$. The left and right sides match identically!
script:
[Prof. Park] On slide 4, let's examine In-Class Practice Problems 3 and 4 from workbook page 19: Problem 3: 3(w - 4) = 3(w - 9) + 15. Problem 4: -4x + 4(x - 4) = -11. Let's solve Problem 3: 3(w - 4) = 3(w - 9) + 15.

[TA Sora] Step 1: Distribute 3 on both sides: Left side: 3 Â· w - 3 Â· 4 = 3w - 12. Right side: 3 Â· w - 3 Â· 9 + 15 = 3w - 27 + 15.

[Prof. Park] Step 2: Combine like terms on the right side: -27 + 15 = -12. Look at our equation now: 3w - 12 = 3w - 12! Both sides are completely identical! Subtract 3w from both sides: -12 = -12. Add 12 to both sides: 0 = 0.

[TA Sora] This is a TRUE statement that holds for every number! Therefore, Problem 3 is an IDENTITY! Solution: All Real Numbers (â)! Now let's tackle Problem 4: -4x + 4(x - 4) = -11. Step 1: Distribute the 4: -4x + 4x - 16 = -11.

[Prof. Park] Step 2: Combine like terms on the left: -4x + 4x = 0! The x terms cancel out to zero! We are left with: -16 = -11. Negative 16 does NOT equal negative 11! This is FALSE! Therefore, Problem 4 is a CONTRADICTION! Classification: Contradiction.

[TA Sora] Solution: No Solution (â). In Practice Problem 3: 3(w - 4) = 3(w - 9) + 15, let's test our identity by plugging in a random number for w, say w = 10: Left side: 3(10 - 4) = 3(6) = 18.

[Prof. Park] Right side: 3(10 - 9) + 15 = 3(1) + 15 = 3 + 15 = 18! 18 = 18! Now test w = -5: Left: 3(-5 - 4) = 3(-9) = -27.

[TA Sora] Right: 3(-5 - 9) + 15 = 3(-14) + 15 = -42 + 15 = -27! -27 = -27! No matter what number you plug inâpositive, negative, fraction, or decimalâboth sides evaluate to the exact same value! That is the living definition of an identity.

title: In-Class Practice #5 & #6
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 12 • Section 1.6 Extra Practice #5 & #6 (Workbook p. 19)
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
pitfall: **Practice #5 Check:** $y = 0$ is a UNIQUE real number solution, so Practice #5 is CONDITIONAL!
script:
[Prof. Park] Slide 5 concludes Lecture 12 with In-Class Practice Problems 5 and 6 from workbook page 19: Problem 5: -(-y - 28) = 7(y + 4). Problem 6: -2(r + 3) + 7 = 1 - 2r. Problem 5 is a favorite exam trap!

[TA Sora] Watch closely: Left side: distribute the negative sign: -(-y) - (-28) = y + 28! Right side: distribute 7: 7 Â· y + 7 Â· 4 = 7y + 28! So our equation is: y + 28 = 7y + 28.

[Prof. Park] Subtract 28 from both sides: y = 7y. Subtract y from both sides: 0 = 6y. Divide by 6: y = 0 / 6 = 0! Students often see 0 = 6y and falsely assume it has no solution or is an identity.

[TA Sora] That is completely wrong! y = 0 is a single, perfectly valid number! If you plug in y = 0: -(-0 - 28) = 28, and 7(0 + 4) = 28. 28 = 28! So Problem 5 is CONDITIONAL, with the single solution y = 0!

[Prof. Park] Now let's solve Problem 6: -2(r + 3) + 7 = 1 - 2r. Distribute -2: -2r - 6 + 7 = 1 - 2r. Combine like terms on the left: -6 + 7 = +1. So the left side is: -2r + 1.

[TA Sora] The right side is: 1 - 2r (which is also -2r + 1)! Both sides are identical! Add 2r to both sides: 1 = 1. This is ALWAYS TRUE! Therefore, Problem 6 is an IDENTITY, with solution All Real Numbers (â)!

[Prof. Park] In Lecture 13, we tackle Section 1.7: Solving Linear Equations with Fractions by Clearing the LCD. Outstanding work on classifying equations today, and see you in Lecture 13!

[TA Sora] Let's review the critical distinction between Problem 5 and Problem 6: In Problem 5, -(-y - 28) = 7(y + 4) led to y = 0. Notice that the variable y did NOT disappear! We had y on the left and 7y on the right: 1y â  7y!

[Prof. Park] Because the coefficients were different (1 vs 7), the variable COULD NOT cancel! Whenever the coefficients of the variable are different on opposite sides of the equation, the equation is GUARANTEED to be conditional and have exactly one unique solution!

[TA Sora] That is a golden rule: Different variable coefficients mean ONE UNIQUE SOLUTION! Identical variable coefficients mean either NO SOLUTION (if constants differ) or ALL REAL NUMBERS (if constants match)! Let's write down this master classification summary in your lecture notebook:
1. Coefficients different: Conditional (e.g.

[Prof. Park] 5x + 2 = 3x - 8 -> 1 solution). 2. Coefficients same, constants different: Contradiction (e.g. 4x + 7 = 4x - 1 -> No Solution â). 3. Coefficients same, constants same: Identity (e.g. 2x + 6 = 2x + 6 -> All Real Numbers â)!

[TA Sora] Memorizing that 3-part classification matrix gives you 100% confidence on any equation classification question on Exam 1!
